messages.subject: Comparison of factor scores of two-dimensional 2PL IRT model
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to scale stereotypes against two different outgroups in the IRT framework. My first approach was to use a bifactorial model, but I discarded that because the general factor sucked up too much variance such that some items loaded negatively on the specific factor. My new approach is to constrain the loadings. More precisely, if I the first six stereotypes are related to the first outgroup and stereotypes 7-12 are related to the second outgroup, I allow for freely estimated covariance between factors and run

model <- mirt.model('F1 = 1-6
F2 = 7-12
COV = F1*F2')

c_mod <- mirt(stereo_type_data, model, printcycles = FALSE) #non-reproducible

My confusion here is the following: Can I substantively compare factor-scores of the two factors produced by this model? I am hesitant because some of the overall item information is represented in the non-factor-specific location, or in mirt syntax difficulty parameter. Is such a comparison of factor scores a reasonable approach to assess stereotypes against two outgroups from a comparative perspective?

Thanks so much,
Tobi

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Comparison of factor scores of two-dimensional 2PL IRT model
parts:
Hi Tobias,

I'm not sure I understand the reason for dropping the bifactor model since negative specific factor slopes are quite common (and generally expected when a small packet is defined). You should stick with the model that makes the most sense theoretically.

In your model though I can't see why you couldn't compare the factor scores, especially since they should be in the same standardized metric. But if you are comparing groups, you should probably use the group argument in bfactor() or the multilpeGroup() functions instead to compare across groups/impose constraints. Cheers.

Phil

Phil

Hi Tobias,

For the first question, your understanding is correct.  The intercept gives the value of theta (your "person location") at which 50% of respondents endorse the correct response.  In a Rasch model, where the slopes are constrained to be equal, this means items can be plotted against each other, like this: http://qssi.psu.edu/images/IRT.jpg The further right the curve, the higher you have to be on the trait to endorse the correct response.  Items to the left are correctly endorsed at lower values of theta and so can be understood as "easier".  But yes, you may have to flip the signs to interpret your data in this manner.

For the second, I don't think you have a grouping variable, and you are using some out of date syntax.  I believe what you are looking for is:

model_2 <- mirt.model()

F1 = 1-6
   F2 = 7-12
   COV = F1*F2

CONSTRAIN = (1-6, a1), (7-12, a1)

c_mod_rasch <- mirt(tobit[,88:99], model_2, verbose = FALSE, rotate = "oblimin", SE = TRUE)

Note: you don't use CONSTRAINB unless you are constraining the parameters between groups.  Also, in both cases we are constraining the slopes across items, so it is fine to use the same name, since we are defining two sets of equality constraints.

Cheers,
Matt

On Mon, Jan 12, 2015 at 10:38 AM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
HI Phil,

After your very helpful hint about the error-prone coding of the group variable, I do have two questions remaining.

First, while the results of the multiplegroup model are now comparable to the separate models, there is still differences of up to .05 in the discrimination parameters. Where do these differences come from?

Different stopping criteria. All models stop when TOL < .0001 by default, but this can occur at different times if they are run separately. You could always drop the TOL criteria further to make them exactly converge (but practically speaking, it really doesn't make any difference).

On a different note, I am now successfully comparing the valence of 7 stereotypes (hispanic-lazy,hispanic-eager etc.) against the valence of 7 other stereotypes (muslim-lazy, muslim-hispanic etc). within the same population by constraining discrimination parameters and looking at the differences in intercepts, as discussed. Because my muslim and hispanic-stereotype items are identical, I wonder whether it would make sense to "rbind" the set of 7 stereotypes each and make use of the multipleGroup option with freed latent means to compare which outgroup is "worse off". Would that make sense you think?

I'm not really sure what you mean, but I don't think I could offer any specific data recommendations anyway. I think you might be on your own in the analysis here, but perhaps posting something to a site like CrossValidated to get other peoples opinions on how to answer your design questions. Cheers.

Phil

Thanks (you will for sure get a huge mention on this project!),
Tobi

group=c (rep ("D1", length (which (data$country=="US"))),

On Thu, Jan 8, 2015 at 5:13 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Phil,

I am struggling a bit as to how to interpret multipleGroup. I am assessing DIF with regard to stereotypes against two outgroups (Factor 1 and Factor 2) in three populations (US, UK, CA).

 I am trying to use (almost exactly) above model, i.e

model_constrained <- mirt.model('
F1 = 1-7
F2 = 8-14
COV = F1*F2
CONSTRAIN = (1-7, a1), (8-14, a2)')
group=c (rep ("D1", length (which (data$country=="US"))),
         rep ("D2", length (which (data$country=="UK"))),
         rep ("D3", length (which (data$country=="CA"))))
mod_metric <- multipleGroup(data[,119:132], model_constrained, group = group,SE=T)


My hope was to directly compare slope-parameters, For example, I would like to say that item one contributes "more" to Factor 1 in group "US" compared to group "UK" because its slope-parameter is more positive. However, running above model gives vastly different answers than running independent models (i.e. for group "US":

model_constrained <- mirt.model('
F1 = 1-7
F2 = 8-14
COV = F1*F2
CONSTRAIN = (1-7, a1), (8-14, a2)')
mod_metric <- mirt(data[which(data$country==US),119:132], model_constrained, group = group,SE=T) 

and I am not sure what I miss. For example, running models separately reveals that perceptions of religious fanaticism are more important to Muslim-stereotyping in the US than in the UK (higher slope parameter), but the Multiple-group option yields the opposite result. I am sure it has something to do with the confirmatory nature of the model. When I run a simple exploratory model, i.e.

group=c (rep ("D1", length (which (data$country=="US"))),
         rep ("D2", length (which (data$country=="UK"))),
         rep ("D3", length (which (data$country=="CA"))))
mod_metric <- multipleGroup(data[,119:132], 1, group = group,SE=T)
mod_metric_separate <- mirt(data[which(data$country==US),119:132], 1, group = group,SE=T)
, the country-specific outputs of mod_metric are comparable with mod_metric_separate.

What am I missing?

Many thanks,
Tobi


On Monday, December 8, 2014 at 9:30:28 AM UTC-5, Phil Chalmers wrote:
Yes that seems like the right interpretation. Multiple-group (MG) methods are essentially a blend between two extremes: no group membership (ignoring it completely in the full datasets) and completely independent groups (equivalent to completely subsetting and analyzing independently with different mirt() runs). MG becomes beneficial when studying the relative equivalence of groups, and also allows linking of the groups by freeing things like latent variances and means (requires a certain amount of item-level constraints; but not many). Cheers.

Phil

I hope you are doing fine!

model_constrained <- mirt.model('
F1 = 1-5
F2 = 6-12
COV = F1*F2
CONSTRAIN = (1-8, a1), (9-16, a2)')


t

Yes the interpretation is fine provided that the average of the first 6 intercepts is higher than the average of the second set. Otherwise, the interpretation is just the opposite.

Phil

Yes, sorry, that was a spelling error on my part. It should have been

 L <- matrix(c(0,rep (-1,6),0,rep (1,6)), nrow=1)
wald(mod_true_rasch_se, L)

and now, the statistic makes sense. Would you agree with the substantive interpretation?

One last, huge thanks!

On Monday, October 13, 2014 9:43:33 PM UTC-7, Tobias Konitzer wrote:
Hi all,

I am trying to scale stereotypes against two different outgroups in the IRT framework. My first approach was to use a bifactorial model, but I discarded that because the general factor sucked up too much variance such that some items loaded negatively on the specific factor. My new approach is to constrain the loadings. More precisely, if I the first six stereotypes are related to the first outgroup and stereotypes 7-12 are related to the second outgroup, I allow for freely estimated covariance between factors and run

model <- mirt.model('F1 = 1-6
F2 = 7-12
COV = F1*F2')

c_mod <- mirt(stereo_type_data, model, printcycles = FALSE) #non-reproducible

My confusion here is the following: Can I substantively compare factor-scores of the two factors produced by this model? I am hesitant because some of the overall item information is represented in the non-factor-specific location, or in mirt syntax difficulty parameter. Is such a comparison of factor scores a reasonable approach to assess stereotypes against two outgroups from a comparative perspective?

Thanks so much,
Tobi
